explanation: Fires on a function word (mostly a preposition or particle: with, in, of, to, for, so) that a preceding head word requires to complete a fixed phrase, e.g. 'complete with', 'replete with', 'rich in', 'engage in', 'yet to', 'failing to', 'except for', 'do so'/'much so', 'presence of'. It is strongest when the head word strongly predicts that word. Smaller offshoots: the colon after metadata labels ('By:', 'title:') and the period in 'Dr.'. Loose collocations ('kinds of', 'happy to') fire only weakly, and free-standing prepositions fire little.

Fires on characters inside random alphanumeric ID or hash strings in URLs and tokens, such as pic.twitter.com/ and t.co short links, YouTube IDs, jsfiddle/jsbin IDs and API keys. It is strongest on a digit near the start of the random code. Ordinary words, including names inside URLs, give little or nothing.

Fires on a highly predictable token inside formulaic or boilerplate text: the ' *' line after '/**' at the top of PHP/Java/JS files, 'Copyright' in assembly attributes, 'localhost' after 'http://', '/TR' in w3.org DTD URLs, 'Lumpur' after 'Kuala', and the '’s' in sentence-initial 'That’s'. The cases have no shared meaning; ordinary prose tokens fire only weakly.

Fires on general head nouns that name a domain or category inside technical, scientific or legal noun phrases, e.g. 'organ' (organ function/dose/fibrosis), 'language' (programming language), 'browser', 'Court' (of Appeal), 'Month', 'antibiotic', 'element', 'IDE', 'Button' in clickedButtonAtIndex. There is no single semantic theme. Expect moderate firing on similar generic nouns in academic text and little elsewhere.

Fires on Wikipedia page and URL structure: most strongly the colon in 'Category:' footer lines at the end of a Wikipedia article (after References), and '/wiki' in wikipedia.org URLs. It fires less on other section headers in that boilerplate ('See also', 'External links') and weakly on the period ending an article's first sentence. Outside Wikipedia-style text it is essentially silent.

Has two unrelated triggers. (1) Code-markup openers in docs: Markdown code fences (```js, ```http, ``) and Rd '\code'. (2) Normative adjectives like 'moral', 'ethical', 'legal' (and 'morality', 'unlawful', 'legitimate'), with weaker firing on 'magnetic'/'magnetism'. The token itself is what matters in both.

A mixture with no clear shared trigger. It fires on quantifiers ('every', 'all', 'any'), on 'where'/'asking' that introduce a clause, on commas after filing dates in patent boilerplate ('filed ... 2000,'), and on leading indentation whitespace in code. It is hard to predict on new text.

Mainly fires on the leading indentation whitespace of the first statement inside a newly opened code block or function body (right after '{' and a newline). It also fires on lambda/arrow parameter closers (') {', ' =>', '|'). A separate trigger: the space between a law-reporter abbreviation and the page number in legal citations ('S.W.3d 26', 'P.2d 372'). Prose gives almost nothing.

Fires most reliably on 'referred' in patent and technical phrasing like '(hereinafter referred to as ...)' and 'variably referred to as'. Many other top examples are unrelated mid-sentence tokens ('going', 'over', 'New' York, 'Python', 'share', 'fit'). Beyond the 'referred to as' cue the unit is not predictable.

A mixture. It fires on the 'of' or comma after attorney names in legal-opinion counsel listings ('McLeroy of Eyster', 'Smithyman, Smithyman &'), the space before a number in citations or labels ('Super. 660', 'Issue 115', 'Season 3'), and words like 'Parameters'/'parameter', 'error', 'icon', 'No.' in technical text. There is no single concept.

Fires on varied tokens inside technical, scientific or news noun phrases: 'Pd' in chemistry, the 'ors' in processors/transistors, 'speed', 'military', 'coach', 'Deputy', 'action', 'activation', 'II' in polymerase II. There is no evident shared semantics, so firing on new text is hard to predict.
